items.text: The evaluation dataset includes approximately 30K total papers from a held-out pool of papers, consisting of 1K query papers and a candidate set of up to 5 cited papers and 25 (randomly selected) uncited papers.
items.why: Describes the candidate set construction and size for direct citation evaluation.
items.plain: The test set has 30,000 papers, with 1,000 query papers that each face up to 5 cited papers and 25 random uncited papers.

items.text: As is typical in clickthrough data on ranked lists, the clicks are biased toward the top of original ranking presented to the user.
items.why: Identifies position bias in recommendation click data.
items.plain: Clicks in recommendation list data naturally favor items shown at the top.

items.text: To counteract this effect, we computed propensity scores using a swap experiment (Agarwal et al., 2019).
items.why: Explains how propensity scores were estimated to fix position bias.
items.plain: They estimated position bias by running a swap test to see how often each list position gets extra clicks purely due to its placement.

items.text: We test different embeddings on the recommendation task by including cosine embedding distance9 as a feature within an existing recommendation system that includes several other informative features (title/author similarity, reference and citation overlap, etc.).
items.why: Details how baseline features are combined with embeddings in recommendations.
items.plain: The recommendation evaluation combines cosine distance of embeddings with existing features like title matching, author matching, and citation overlap.

items.text: We empirically found it helpful to use 2 hard negatives (citations of citations) and 3 easy negatives (randomly selected papers) for each query paper.
items.why: Specifies the ratio of hard to easy negative samples during pretraining.
items.plain: For each search paper, training used 2 hard negative papers (citations of citations) and 3 easy negative papers (randomly picked).

items.text: We perform minimal tuning of our model’s hyperparameters based on the performance on the validation set, while baselines are extensively tuned.
items.why: Reveals unequal hyperparameter tuning between SPECTER and baselines.
items.plain: They tuned SPECTER's hyperparameters only minimally using a validation set, whereas they tuned the comparison methods extensively.

items.text: We train the model on a single Titan V GPU (12G memory) for 2 epochs, with batch size of 4 (the maximum that ﬁt in our GPU memory) and use gradient accumulation for an effective batch size of 32.
items.why: Reports a small physical batch size forced by GPU memory limits.
items.plain: Hardware constraints capped the physical batch size at 4, though gradient accumulation built an effective batch size of 32.

items.text: We compare with several strong textual models: SIF (Arora et al., 2017), a method for learning document representations by removing the ﬁrst principal component of aggregated word-level embeddings which we pretrain on scientiﬁc text; SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019) a state-of-the-art pretrained Transformer LM for scientiﬁc text; and Sent-BERT (Reimers and Gurevych, 2019), a model that uses negative sampling to tune BERT for producing optimal sentence embeddings.
items.why: Lists key text-based baseline models compared in the evaluation.
items.plain: They compared against text models including SIF pretrained on scientific text, SciBERT, and Sent-BERT.

items.text: We also compare with Citeomatic (Bhagavatula et al., 2018), a closely related paper representation model for citation prediction which trains content-based representations with citation graph information via dynamically sampled triplets, and SGC (Wu et al., 2019a), a state-of-the-art graph-convolutional approach.
items.why: Lists content-graph and graph-convolutional baselines.
items.plain: They also compared against Citeomatic, which samples citation triplets, and SGC, a graph convolution model.

items.text: virtually all other baselines except for SGC, which has access to the citation graph at training and test time.12 Note that methods like SGC cannot be used in real-world setting to embed new papers that are not cited yet.
items.why: Explains why graph baseline SGC cannot embed uncited paper test cases.
items.plain: Graph methods like SGC cannot generate embeddings for brand new papers that lack existing citations.

items.text: On the recommendations task, as opposed to previous experiments, the differences in method scores are generally smaller.
items.why: Notes smaller performance gaps in recommendation due to extra non-embedding features.
items.plain: Performance differences between models shrink on the recommendation task because the system relies on multiple other strong features alongside embeddings.

items.text: We performed an online A/B test comparing our SPECTER-based recommender to an existing production recommender system for similar papers that ranks papers by a textual similarity measure.
items.why: States the online A/B test baseline was textual similarity, not a top model.
items.plain: The live A/B test compared SPECTER against a production system that ranked papers using a basic text similarity measure.

items.text: 12For SGC, we remove development and test set citations and co-citations during training.
items.why: Explains how evaluation citations were masked during SGC graph baseline training.
items.plain: To evaluate SGC fairly, the authors removed validation and test citation links during model training.

items.text: More surprisingly, adding authors as an input (along with title and abstract) hurts performance.13 One possible explanation is that author names are sparse in the corpus, making it difﬁcult for the model to infer document-level relatedness from them.
items.why: Hypothesizes why adding author names degraded embedding performance in ablations.
items.plain: Adding author metadata might hurt performance because rare author names make it hard to infer paper relationships.

items.text: Many author names are out-of-vocabulary for SciBERT and thus, they might be split into sub-words and shared across names that are not semantically related, leading to noisy correlation.
items.why: Identifies sub-word tokenization of names as a potential confound in metadata ablations.
items.plain: Sub-word tokenization might split unfamiliar author names into generic pieces, creating false connections between unrelated people.

items.text: 14Venue information in our data came directly from publisher provided metadata and thus was not normalized.
items.why: Notes unnormalized venue metadata as a limitation in venue ablations.
items.plain: Publisher venue names were not standardized, which may explain why adding venue information failed to help.

items.text: The ﬁfth row of Table 2 shows that this is important—using only easy negatives reduces performance on all tasks.
items.why: Shows that removing hard negatives degrades performance across all benchmark tasks.
items.plain: Training with only random negative examples reduces overall performance on every task.

items.text: The sixth row of the table shows that using a strong general-domain language model (BERT-Large) instead of SciBERT in SPECTER reduces performance considerably.
items.why: Shows that replacing domain SciBERT with general BERT-Large reduces accuracy.
items.plain: Starting from a general BERT-Large model instead of domain-specific SciBERT substantially degrades model performance.

items.text: We experiment with ﬁne-tuning SciBERT on our tasks, and ﬁnd this to be generally inferior to using our ﬁxed representations from SPECTER.
items.why: Claims fixed SPECTER embeddings outperform direct task-specific fine-tuning.
items.plain: Fine-tuning SciBERT directly on target tasks yields worse performance than using SPECTER's fixed paper embeddings.

items.text: SPECTER embeddings are based on only the title and abstract of the paper.
items.why: Acknowledges limitation of using only title and abstract instead of full text.
items.plain: SPECTER builds representations using only paper titles and abstracts.

items.text: Further, modern language models have strict memory limits on input size, which means new techniques would be required in order to leverage the entirety of the paper within the models.
items.why: Identifies Transformer memory limits as a technical barrier to processing full text.
items.plain: Strict memory limits in Transformer LMs prevent directly inputting an entire research paper.

items.text: We found that these pretrained embeddings substantially outperform alternative off-theshelf embeddings.
items.why: Claims custom fasttext embeddings substantially outperformed off-the-shelf alternatives.
items.plain: The authors found that their custom-trained word embeddings worked significantly better than ready-to-use off-the-shelf embeddings.

items.text: An alternative comparison would have been Graph- SAGE (Hamilton et al., 2017b), but SGC (with no learning) outperformed an unsupervised variant of GraphSAGE on the Reddit dataset16, Note that SGC with no learning boils down to graph propagation on node features (in our case nodes are academic documents).
items.why: Justifies choosing SGC over GraphSAGE based on performance on a non-academic dataset.
items.plain: The authors chose SGC over GraphSAGE because an unlearned version of SGC beat an unsupervised GraphSAGE on the Reddit dataset.

items.text: SciBERT To isolate the advantage of SPECTER’s citation-based ﬁne-tuning objective, we add a controlled comparison with SciBERT (Beltagy et al., 2019).
items.why: Defines the specific baseline comparison used to isolate the effect of fine-tuning.
items.plain: To isolate the benefit of their citation-based fine-tuning objective, the authors compared their model against SciBERT.

items.text: 17We also tried the alternative of averaging all token representations, but this resulted in a slight performance decrease compared with the [CLS] pooled token.
items.why: Reports a negative result from an alternative aggregation method.
items.plain: Averaging all token representations performed slightly worse than taking the representation of the single [CLS] token.

items.text: The model is designed to encode sentences as opposed to paragraphs, so we embed the title and each sentence in the abstract separately, sum the embeddings, and L2 normalize the result to produce a ﬁnal 768-dimensional paper embedding.18
items.why: Explains a manual adaptation to apply a sentence-level baseline to whole papers.
items.plain: Because Sentence BERT is built for sentences rather than full documents, the authors embedded the title and abstract sentences separately, summed them, and normalized the vector to create a 768-dimensional paper embedding.
